solution: Multiply each bracket by the fraction in front of it, term by term. The first bracket gives $\dfrac{1}{{=p}}({=A}x-{=B}y)={=a}x-{=b}y$, and the second gives $\dfrac{1}{{=q}}({=C}x+{=D}y)={=c}x+{=b}y$.
Write the two results as one sum: $\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{{=p}}({=A}x-{=B}y)+\dfrac{1}{{=q}}({=C}x+{=D}y)&={=a}x-{=b}y+{=c}x+{=b}y\end{aligned}$
Collect like terms. The $y$ terms cancel because $-{=b}y+{=b}y=0$, and the $x$ terms give ${=a}x+{=c}x={=T}x$.
notes: Models the book's own twist in ex1-11-23i (page 38): fractional coefficients that divide each bracket exactly, so every term becomes a whole-number coefficient, and the y terms cancel in the sum, leaving a single x term. Construction: bracket coefficients are p*a, p*b and q*c, q*b, so the division is always exact and the two y coefficients are always equal and opposite (the book's -9y and +18y become -3y and +3y). a, b, c are at least 2 so no instance prints a coefficient of 1. p and q always differ (the book uses 3 and 6). Answer is the single term (a+c)x; the marker lists y among the variables because it appears in the stem. No distractors (expression type), so no misconception ids are needed; the catalogue for this objective is empty. I checked 3000 sampled instances numerically: stem, every equality in the solution steps, and the marker answer agree at four test points.
